cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Hand It Over
cards.instruction: Persuade someone to give up control of a task, object, or decision you believe is being mishandled.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I've reviewed your seating plan. The exes together are not approved; you may hand me the pencil.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Can they stay? They're civil now.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Civility is approved from separate tables. Let me move just those two names.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I've spent hours balancing the rest of it.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: The rest has provisional approval. You may watch me change only those two places; then you can explain the balance while I hold the pencil.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 withholds seating approval and asks the pencil; A3 approves civility only apart; A5 conditionally preserves other work while seeking control.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 civility defense causes A3 limited two-name proposal; B4 investment concern causes A5 watched limited edits and explanation under A supervision.

relationship.evidence: B2 defends the judgment and B4 protects work invested, giving A specific concerns to address rather than mere refusal.

heightening.evidence: B4 balancing concern becomes A5 a concrete limited-change concession that still places the decision tool with A.

specificity.evidence: A1 exes seated together and B4 hours balancing establish the perceived mishandling and cost of surrendering control.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 holding the pencil while B explains makes the limited concession reveal A continuing control.
